title: Ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli bacteremia from pyelonephritis on ceftriaxone

clinical_review.notes: Owner approved revision 2 of the M6 library-growth draft (with OpenEvidence's review).

story: A 76-year-old woman with urosepsis from pyelonephritis (no urinary catheter) is on IV ceftriaxone. On hospital day 2 blood and urine grow E. coli resistant to ceftriaxone, cefepime, ciprofloxacin and TMP-SMX and susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, ertapenem and meropenem. She is still febrile; her creatinine is normal for her.

results.text: Leukocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count

cultures.order_text: Bacteria identified in Blood by Culture

expected_findings.summary: The blood E. coli is resistant to ceftriaxone, her current therapy, and she remains febrile.

reference_answer: Change to a carbapenem: ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours (500 mg daily at a creatinine clearance of 30 or below), or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours (renally adjusted) if critically ill or hypoalbuminemic (IDSA 2026 Question 1.3). Piperacillin-tazobactam, although susceptible, is not suggested with concomitant bacteremia (Question 1.4). No oral option is active for this isolate; IDSA allows oral non-beta-lactam step-down when one is susceptible. About 7 days from the first effective dose if she improves (IDSA 2025 cUTI with bacteremia).
rationale: A bug-drug mismatch on a blood isolate; the library's other mismatch case is urine only.

citations.supports: Questions 1.3 and 1.4: carbapenems preferred outside the urinary tract and with bacteremia; piperacillin-tazobactam only for ESBL cUTI without bacteremia in patients not critically ill; checked against IDSA's 2026 text 2026-11-12.
7 days for complicated UTI with Gram-negative bacteremia when improving; checked against IDSA's PDF 2026-11-12.
Prospective audit and feedback of antibiotic therapy as a stewardship intervention.
